blocks.source: Vol III, Test-Time Compute, § Selecting from a Candidate Pool
blocks.md: Sampling eight candidate patches for the connection pool helps nothing if seven of them repeat the same broken timeout workaround and the selector picks one of the seven over the single patch that fixes the notification bug. In a typical pool, one candidate might lengthen an acquisition timeout, another might add exponential retries, and a third might change how the connection-return path wakes waiting threads.

questions.q: The section **Selecting from a Candidate Pool** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: A step check that rejects a fraction r of b children gives an effective branching factor b(1-r), so a tree stays finite on its own only when r > 1-1/b and otherwise needs hard caps.
A search tracks money, non-interchangeable work, wall time, and peak live state in separate accounts and reserves each request's maximum charge before dispatch, releasing it only on settlement.
Recording a candidate as a dependency graph of artifacts with evidence provenance lets a refuting observation invalidate exactly its descendants while retained branches keep their support.

pass@k = 1-(1-p)^k caps any selector that returns an unchanged pool member, while realized accuracy is set by the selector, so coverage near 98 percent can coexist with a vote that plateaus near half.
